title: Bountiful
summary: Turn every market in to a shop
description:
As somebody who loves to travel around Asia, it's always very difficult to buy local. We use the video understanding models to convert video footage of markets into real high-quality e-commerce stores so that local people can reach travelers and expats, investing more dollars into local economies. 

Built today on the event stack: walkthrough videos go into our team's VAST S3 bucket; on the workshop VM each video is cut into 5-second pieces, NVIDIA Cosmos Reason on CoreWeave GPUs lists every item for sale, Llama 3.3 70B on Weights & Biases Inference turns that into clean catalogue entries, Cosmos Embed1 indexes every item and moment, and it all lives in VastDB. The shop reads that catalogue: 97 pieces from markets in New York, Bali and Chiang Mai, each linked to the exact 5 seconds it appears on camera. A 60-second walkthrough takes about 90 to 120 s of compute on one worker and scales out linearly.

title: Sentiment Engine
summary: A real-time video agent that pairs on-screen game events with players' facial reactions and makes hours of gameplay searchable in plain language.
description:
Sentiment Engine turns gaming reaction videos into searchable, time-indexed intelligence by pairing what happens on screen with how the player reacts.

For any gameplay video, SE finds the moments that matter — the in-game event (the stimulus) and the player's facial expression at that instant (the response) — then lets you search hours of footage in plain language and auto-writes a studio insight brief when something lands.

How it works:

Ingest — yt-dlp pulls the video stream; ffmpeg samples frames.
Game understanding — NVIDIA model captions the on-screen event per window.
Reaction lane — SE locates the creator's webcam corner, crops the player's face at each event, and the VLM reads the facial expression + intensity.
Fusion — events × reaction intensity × cross-video synchrony rank the "notable moments."
Action — NVIDIA model writes a 2-sentence design/marketing brief for the top moment.
Search — plain-language queries return the moment + reaction.

title: Vision Zero Agent
summary: Real-time alerts for news desks facing hours of raw footage: NVIDIA Cosmos checks every 5 s segment as it arrives for the event you describe (explosions: 51 of 56 found), and the same agent flags close calls on street and warehouse cameras.
description:
A news desk gets hours of raw footage from remote cameras in conflict zones and disaster areas, two or three hours per feed. Somewhere inside are the five seconds that matter. Nobody can watch every feed live.

Vision Zero Agent watches for them. It cuts each incoming feed into 5 s segments and sends each one to NVIDIA Cosmos Reason on CoreWeave GPUs as it arrives. When Cosmos sees the event, the agent saves the clip and alerts the desk: a pop-up and chime on the page, a desktop notification, and an email or webhook. The event is just a prompt: we built and measured it on explosions, and the same trigger can watch for fires, floods, building collapses or crowd surges.

Measured on public-domain Wikimedia Commons war films: 51 of 56 explosions found in 222 hand-checked clips (91% recall, 85% precision). On three films it had never seen, every blast raised a live alert, with 0 false alarms in 36 segments. Known limits: it misses the first flash before the cloud forms, and confuses parachutes with bombs.

The same agent protects people on everyday cameras. Across 3,500+ street and warehouse clips stored and searched on VAST, it flags cars cutting close to pedestrians and cyclists, and workers in the path of forklifts and robots (8/10 and 6/6 agree with human review). Reviewers confirm alerts, plain-English watch rules search the archive (gpt-oss-120b on W&B Inference), and one click writes an incident report. Every call is traced in W&B Weave. Built in one day with Cursor.

title: RehabNinja
summary: AI enabled rehab game
description:
Rehab is boring and requires grit most people don’t have two weeks after surgery. The day-7 “how are you walking?” call hears “fine,” and decline shows up later—in the ED.

Rise turns post-op check-ins into RehabNinja: stand in front of your phone, do today’s move, and clean reps slice fruit on your joints. Knees cave in or you push off with your hands—and the fruit becomes a bomb. Patients only see hits, misses, and a plain coach. Behind the game, the same camera pose tracking runs a CDC STEADI–style chair stand so the care team gets real function, trend vs last time, and a deterministic triage card (escalate, nurse callback, or continue)—rules-first, human-approved, never model-written patient copy.

Built for the VAST Real-Time Video Agents Hack (NYC). On-device pose (YOLO with MediaPipe fallback), spoken + captioned coaching, red-flag symptoms that jump straight to emergency instructions. All patients are synthetic. Play it like a game; measure it like rehab.

title: AisleGuard
summary: AisleGuard is an autonomous warehouse safety agent that detects worker–forklift proximity risks, searches historical video for similar incidents, and triggers alerts when recurring hazards emerge.
description:
AisleGuard is an autonomous warehouse safety agent that turns passive video footage into actionable safety intelligence. It identifies worker–forklift proximity events, uses NVIDIA Cosmos and YOLO11 to understand what is happening in the footage, and searches the VAST video archive for similar historical incidents. AisleGuard then uses Weights & Biases serverless inference on CoreWeave-powered infrastructure to reason across the current event and related evidence, determine whether the behavior represents a recurring hazard, and automatically generate a safety alert with a recommended action.
Instead of forcing safety teams to manually review hours of warehouse footage, AisleGuard lets them investigate incidents, search the archive in plain language, ask questions about past events, and surface patterns that may otherwise go unnoticed. The result is a real-time video agent that can detect, retrieve, reason, and act—helping teams identify recurring operational risks before they lead to more serious incidents.

title: Visual Actions
summary: It's a menu bar app that controls the desktop with gestures, using modes the way Vim does. You raise an open palm to "arm" it, then make a command gesture:
description: 1. Perception: MediaPipe Hand Landmarker reads 21 hand landmarks from each OpenCV webcam frame. We turn them into a 65-number feature vector. 2. Classification: A scikit-learn logistic regression, trained on public HaGRIDv2 landmarks plus synthetic and calibration data, labels each frame. A hold timer weighted by confidence keeps random hand movement from firing commands. 3. Action: PyObjC calls macOS directly (Quartz events, the Accessibility API, overlays). It sends keystrokes, moves windows with its own snapping, and draws on-screen feedback. 4. Self-improvement loop (the hackathon part): Every gesture event is logged. The intent pipeline goes segments → video clips → Cosmos Reason → JEV check → tagger → review → export: - Cosmos Reason (the shared NIM, cosmos3-nano-reasoner) watches each clip and judges what the user meant to do: a real command, a misfire, or a missed gesture. - A JEV pass (over OpenRouter) cross-checks Cosmos's verdict. - An LLM tagger with escalation to a stronger model settles disagreements and writes corrected labels. - The corrected labels go back into retraining.

title: Sightline
summary: Self-configuring video agents that understand any feed, decide what matters, and automatically monitor, investigate, and mark important moments.
description:
Sightline turns any video feed into a self-configuring monitoring agent. Instead of making users define rules, detectors, or searches, Sightline first watches the footage, identifies the environment and important entities, decides what events matter, and writes its own NVIDIA Cosmos analysis prompt.  
Users can search the VAST archive and click “Add to Monitor,” or upload a completely new clip. Sightline then configures itself for that feed, monitors it, places events directly on a scrubbable timeline, and investigates important moments using before/after context, YOLO detections, related footage, other camera angles, a Cosmos second look, and a W&B reasoning verdict.  
The same engine adapts across environments: a warehouse feed generated worker/forklift safety objectives, while street footage generated pedestrian/vehicle objectives. Sightline uses VAST Data, NVIDIA Cosmos Reason + Embed, YOLO11, CoreWeave, Weights & Biases Inference, and Cursor.

title: Exhibit A
summary: Put a claim about your video archive on trial: one agent prosecutes with search, another cross-examines every exhibit against physical evidence, a judge rules, and the tape itself takes the stand. Nothing counts until it survives.
description:
**Put a claim about your video archive on trial: one agent prosecutes with search, another cross-examines every exhibit against physical evidence, a judge rules, and the tape itself takes the stand. Nothing counts until it survives.**Video search runs on captions, and captions are written by a model under someone else's prompt. They hallucinate (a "truck in the bike lane" that is really a bus at a stop) and they leave out whatever the prompt never asked about. Every search tool today asks you to believe them. Exhibit A refuses. This tool is useful for investigations and for analyzing relevant evidence. This is helpful for security and safety applications as well as efficiency.

**Video index.** Video search runs against the VAST VSS retrieval API 
**Captions and embeddings.** Captions come from NVIDIA Cosmos3-Reason (cosmos3-nano-reasoner) and embeddings from Cosmos-Embed1,
**Detections.** A YOLO11 (COCO-80) sidecar provides max-per-frame counts, boxes for the densest frame, and frames-seen per class.
**Tape witness.** The tape witness is Cosmos3-Reason 
**Courtroom agents.** The courtroom roles run on Weights & Biases serverless inference: Llama 3.1 8B plays the prosecutor and bailiff, and Llama 3.3 70B plays the defense and judge.

title: PharOS
summary: PharOS turns NYC’s traffic cameras into an early-warning system for city safety teams, spotting near misses and risky behavior at intersections so dangerous corners can be fixed before the next crash.
description:
NYC DOT’s traffic cameras watch the city’s most dangerous corners but record nothing, so every near miss is lost. PharOS is a 3D map of Manhattan with a heatmap of injury crashes from the last 12 months of NYC Open Data, and every node is a real DOT camera. Open an intersection to see its camera image, crash history, reported causes, crashes by hour, and next steps. For continuous video, PharOS monitors live 511NY feeds and returns a verdict on each 8-second clip in about 14 seconds. Plain-English search finds matching moments in recorded footage.

How we used the stack:

VAST AI OS: The workshop’s VAST pipeline had already indexed recorded New York footage into VastDB. PharOS queries it with hybrid semantic search and streams matching clips for seekable playback.

NVIDIA: On each live clip, YOLO11 boxes every car, person and bike across 32 frames, while Cosmos Reason reads the same video and describes what happened. Neither can claim motion from a single frame.

CoreWeave: Its GPUs serve the NVIDIA models, which return results in under 3 seconds.

Weights & Biases: W&B Inference runs Llama 3.3 70B. It turns each clip’s findings into a structured verdict, turns questions into search plans, and writes next steps linked to official guidance.

Next: live video at every DOT camera, and a citywide ranking of intersections by near misses for planners.

pageSections.title: Technical architecture
pageSections.body: Every thirty seconds, our backend captures eight seconds of live video at four frames a second. NVIDIA runs two models on that exact clip in parallel. YOLO11 boxes every car, person and bike across all 32 frames, and Cosmos Reason watches the clip and describes what actually happened. Both are served on CoreWeave GPUs and come back in under three seconds. Weights & Biases Inference runs Llama 3.3 70B, which checks those findings against our evidence rules and writes a structured verdict. It also turns plain-English questions into search plans. Those searches run on VAST's video search, which finds and streams matching clips from recorded New York footage.

pageSections.title: Lessons learned
pageSections.body: The hardest lesson was that an AI model will confidently describe a near miss it can’t actually see. Early on, Cosmos labeled a single frame a conflict, so we added a rule that any motion claim needs evidence across several frames. Data access shaped the product more than models did. NYC DOT’s cameras only give still images, so we had to find continuous 511NY video feeds. A packaged FFmpeg also crashed on those streams until we switched decoders. We learned to keep three things separate: a search result is a candidate, a crash count is history, and only a verdict on real footage is an observation. title: FightLens
summary: FightLens helps boxing and MMA viewers understand fast exchanges through AI-powered action tracking, contextual explanations, and evolving win-probability estimates in one viewing interface.
description:
FightLens is an app that helps viewers understand what is happening in boxing and MMA, and why the balance of a fight is changing. It brings fighter tracking, exchange analysis, and win-probability estimates into one interface, with corresponding video moments viewers can revisit to inspect the evidence.

Our event-driven pipeline separates fast action detection, contextual video understanding, and decision updates. YOLO acts as an always-on sentinel, tracking fighters and flagging potential attacks. When an exchange is detected, NVIDIA Cosmos receives a clip with context before and after the trigger to interpret the action and generate an explanation. This design aims to reduce redundant video-model calls without missing brief exchanges.

VAST Data organizes video features, real-time events, and related data into shared context for prediction. The Jev architecture with clef-flash supports rapid updates to the estimated advantage. Each exchange, explanation, and probability update is linked so viewers can follow the reasoning.

The displayed probabilities are prototype estimates, not yet validated or calibrated. Next, we plan to use historical fight videos to evaluate and improve the workflow, measuring end-to-end latency and prediction quality separately. Our team combines boxing experience, AI research, and product development to make combat sports easier to follow.

pageSections.title: Technical architecture
pageSections.body: Video stream → YOLO fighter tracking and potential-attack detection → event-triggered clips with pre/post-action context → NVIDIA Cosmos exchange analysis and captions → Jev / clef-flash decision updates → viewer-facing explanations and win-probability estimates. VAST Data provides shared context across video features, events, and related data. The two-branch design keeps lightweight detection running continuously while invoking video understanding around relevant exchanges. Latency and prediction quality will be evaluated separately; probability calibration remains future work.

summary: Spatial Video Agent lets safety and incident investigators ask one plain question across every camera and get the exact moments back, with distances in meters where the camera geometry supports it
description: Spatial Video Agent answers one plain-English question across every camera in the corpus: 3,537 clips from warehouses, a Toronto dashcam, and New York and San Francisco street corners. For each hit, it runs tracking and geometry at query time and returns an answer card grouped by evidence level. Where a camera has calibration or GPS, the card shows the person-to-vehicle distance in meters with an uncertainty. Where it has neither, the agent abstains and says “no geometry”. Video and detections live in VAST S3, and captions and Cosmos embeddings are read live from VastDB on every query. NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Reason and Cosmos-Embed1 run on CoreWeave GPUs. Our FastAPI app runs on the CoreWeave cluster. W&B Weave traces every agent step. Every number comes from CV and geometry, not from the model.

title: StreetCast
summary: StreetCast turns New York street video into cited, ready-to-file 311 reports. A rider's footage becomes every blocked bike lane, trash pile and obstruction, with the clip and the truck's fleet number, never a plate. A newsroom picks a block and gets a narrated segment where every line cites a clip.
description:
StreetCast turns hours of street video into a cited record of what's blocking New York's streets, and helps people act on it.

For riders (Ride report): a delivery cyclist records her ride. StreetCast replays it and every problem lands as a field note: blocked bike lanes, double parking, trash, obstructions, graffiti, construction. Each one comes with a drafted 311 complaint: category, street, what happened, the company and fleet number, and a link to the exact clip. It also shows how much time she lost and what caused it. Fleet numbers, never license plates: accountability for companies, privacy for people.

For newsrooms (Your Block): a producer picks a neighborhood, a time of day and a travel mode. StreetCast runs six searches across the footage and builds a one-minute narrated segment. Every sentence cites the clip and time range it came from. No clip, no sentence.

Eval: claims are checked against the clips they cite, and we report the grounding rate.

How it works: VAST stores, indexes and searches the footage in VastDB. NVIDIA Cosmos Reason describes every clip, Cosmos Embed powers the search, and YOLO11 detects objects. An LLM on W&B Inference turns those descriptions into structured events and scripts, with every call traced in Weave. Built with Cursor.

Rider files it. The city sees it. The newsroom airs it.

The technology stack brings together:

title: Witness — AI-Powered Video Evidence Intelligence
summary: Witness helps accident investigators and claims reviewers evaluate conflicting statements against timestamped video evidence using VAST DataEngine, NVIDIA Cosmos, and YOLO11, with human oversight.
description:
**Witness - Evidence Over Assumptions****
**When drivers provide conflicting accounts of an incident, investigators need a reliable way to examine what video footage actually shows. Manually reviewing recordings, locating important moments, and comparing statements can be time-consuming.

Witness is an AI-assisted video evidence review platform designed to make that process faster, more transparent, and easier to audit.

**What we built:**
Witness provide a web-based investigation workspace featuring:
1. Video evidence playback: Stream footage from VAST storage and navigate the recording using clickable, timestamped evidence markers.
2. Claim verification: Compare individual statements with available video observations and classify each as Supported, Contradicted, or Not Visible
3. NVIDIA Cosmos reasoning: Identify vehicles, pedestrians, traffic signals, and other visible objects as additional context.
4. YOLO11 object detection: This identifies the actual vehicles, pedestrians, traffic signals, and other visible objects as additional context.
5. Evidence inspection: Present claim-specific timestamps, supporting observations, contradiction cues, and explanations in a unified interface.
6. Human Oversight: Clearly distinguish observed evidence from AI-generated interpretations. Witness does not automatically determine legal fault or liability.

title: CloseCall
summary: CloseCall turns the street video cities already have into measured, clip-linked evidence of near misses (close passes, cars in crosswalks, traffic squeezing work-zone flaggers) so Vision Zero and transportation teams can fix the right streets and prove the fixes worked.
description: CloseCall finds **near misses** in the street video cities already have. NVIDIA VSS searches the VAST library (3,537 clips, 13 cameras), YOLO11 boxes every car, bike and person and uses their real size to measure gaps in metres, and NVIDIA Cosmos describes each clip so we can **flag hazards like a car in the crosswalk**. Each clip gets a **0 to 10 danger score**, places are ranked as hotspots, and a person approves every finding against its clip.

pageSections.title: Technical architecture
pageSections.body: A single Python server (standard library only) and a one-page web app, deployed to Kubernetes on the event’s VAST cluster. The server calls the NVIDIA VSS API to search clips and fetch Cosmos descriptions and YOLO11 detections, turns box sizes into gap estimates in metres, scores each clip 0 to 10 and groups clips into hotspots. Findings, review decisions and blind ratings are saved as JSON files; raw video stays in VAST and is streamed through a proxy.

pageSections.title: Setup instructions
pageSections.body: On the event build machine: clone github.com/Sebilopez1/closecall, then run bash deploy/deploy.sh. It reads the team’s VSS credentials from /config, stores them in a Kubernetes Secret, and deploys the server and web app. Open the app URL and press Re-scan footage to search and score the cameras. bash deploy/logs.sh shows the logs. Set CLOSECALL_CAMERA to scan a single camera.

pageSections.title: Lessons learned
pageSections.body: Cosmos describes, it doesn’t measure: we needed YOLO boxes to get distances, and Cosmos to say what was happening. Using an object’s real size as a ruler works, but single-camera gaps are only good to about ±30-50% until a camera is calibrated. Showing every finding with its clip and logging a human decision made results easy to check. We also dropped an early multi-agent build plan for one simple server we could deploy in a minute.

title: Occlusive Logic
summary: Occlusive Logic transforms video object detections into user-programmable spatial rules, enabling anyone to monitor defined areas and generate evidence-backed alerts without retraining AI models.
description:
Traditional computer vision systems can identify objects but understanding when their presence is relevant often requires some custom programming for each application. Occlusive Logic bridges that gap by allowing users to turn existing video detections into configurable, actionable rules. Users select a video source, draw a polygonal zone directly over the footage, choose the object classes, and configure confitions such as entering an area, remaining there for a specified duration, or being absent. A custom Python rules engine evaluates the object positions, confidence thresholds, the tracking informations and temporal conditions to determine when a rule has been satisfied. 
When triggered, the system creates a time stamped incident ticket with visual evidence. Users can inspect, revisit, and resolve incidents through a web dashboard. 
The application integrates with VAST's video infrastructure and uses YOLO detection metadata from VAST provided footage. It is built with Python, FastAPI, Javascript, SQLite, and a custom geometry and temporal state engine. Additional simulations demonstrate potential applications in accessibility focused occlusion monitoring and in proper waste management. 
Computer Engineering foundation: Occlusive logic treats camera detections as virtual sensor signals and applies programmable spatial and sequential logic to produce an event. This lays a foundation for future boolean rule composition and edge hardware deployment.

pageSections.title: Technical architecture
pageSections.body: Occlusive Logic uses a modular video-processing architecture: 1. Perception: YOLO object detections and bounding boxes retrieved alongside VAST-hosted video clips. 2. Spatial processing: User-defined polygonal zones with configurable object-position matching and confidence thresholds. 3. Temporal rule engine: A Python stateful evaluator supporting entry detection, dwell thresholds, absence conditions, object tracking, and event cooldowns. 4. Incident management: FastAPI and SQLite store timestamped incidents, visual evidence, and resolution status. 5. Interface: JavaScript-based dashboard for video playback, zone drawing, rule configuration, and incident review. The perception layer is separ

pageSections.title: Setup instructions
pageSections.body: Source code: https://github.com/rwezzy/ZoneLogic-Tripwire Clone the repository, install the Python dependencies listed in requirements.txt, and run the application using the instructions in README.md. The application includes built-in simulation scenarios that work without external credentials. For VAST footage, configure the required VAST service credentials in the environment and use the VAST video catalog within the application. The VAST integration depends on access to the event infrastructure.

pageSections.title: Lessons learned
pageSections.body: One of the biggest challenges was translating object detections into meaningful events. Detecting a person or vehicle is not enough; the system must determine where an object is, how long it remains there, and whether a rule has actually been violated. I learned the importance of separating perception from decision-making, handling imperfect tracking data, and testing spatial and temporal logic against real video detections rather than relying exclusively on simulations. The project also revealed a promising connection to digital design: object detections can function as virtual sensor signals, opening the possibility of combining them through Boolean logic and sequential state machines. title: SecondCall
summary: SecondCall turns the sports videos sitting in your camera roll into an instant, judge-blind second opinion: it hears and sees the decisive moment, checks it against the rulebook, and shows players and referees the evidence behind each call, starting with kendo.
description:
**Problem.** In sports with judges, calls happen in a split second and people argue about them all the time. Friends and parents film every game, but those videos just sit in our camera rolls. We started with kendo because we both do it: a point only counts if the shout, the strike and the stomp all land in the same quarter-second.

**What it does**. Drop in a match video and SecondCall judges each strike: POINT, NO POINT or CAN'T TELL, with how sure it is and the proof. It also catches penalties (hansoku) and points the referees might have missed.

How it works. First it listens: the stomp and the shinai crack tell us exactly when the strike happened, and NVIDIA Canary hears which target was called. YOLO11 zooms in on the two players and blocks out the referees, then NVIDIA Cosmos looks at the frames around that moment. A rule card turns all that into a verdict, W&B Inference explains it in plain words, and Weave tracks every step. The app never sees the referees' flags, so it can't be swayed by them. Rulings live in VastDB, matches are searchable in VAST Video Search & Summary, and it all runs on CoreWeave GPUs.

Beyond kendo. Every sport is just a new rule card, so it works for judo, fencing, pickleball line calls, or any sport where calls get argued.

What we learned. Plain 5-second clips kept missing the strike. Listening for the moment first, then showing Cosmos close-up frames, fixed it.

Limits. It's a second opinion, not a replacement for referees. Built with Cursor.

title: Witness desk
summary: Witness desk searches every camera in New York or San Francisco for one vehicle by color, body type, and time, then lets you mark the clip and keep a still.
description:
Witness desk is for someone who saw a vehicle and needs the footage. They choose the city, an optional time, the body type, and the color. The desk searches the indexed archive and lays the closest clips out as a network. The lit node plays in place. Yes keeps a still with the case. No clears that clip and moves to the next.

The search uses the stored clip descriptions from the video stack. The desk shows those captions and does not invent events they do not contain. Plates and make or model are not in this index, so the form does not ask for them. Stolen and hit-and-run are marks a person sets after watching a clip. They are not part of the query.

CoreWeave hosts the video models inside that search stack. It shows the captions those models already wrote. Cases stay in the browser, and the live site needs no login.

pageSections.title: Technical architecture
pageSections.body: The Next.js app on Vercel calls the VAST video search API from server routes, so the API token never reaches the browser. Search sends a color and vehicle query, a city metadata filter, and either the whole archive or a time window in that city's timezone. Playback is proxied through the app. The interface turns the returned clips into a node network. Cases and stills stay in the browser.

pageSections.title: Setup instructions
pageSections.body: The repository is public at https://github.com/freeslugs/witness-desk and the live site is https://witness-desk.vercel.app. To run it locally, set VSS_BACKEND, VSS_USERNAME, and VSS_PASSWORD, then run npm install and npm run dev. Do not commit those credentials.

pageSections.title: Lessons learned
pageSections.body: A specific vehicle question fits this footage better than a free-text hunt. Color, body type, city, and an optional time window are what the captions can answer. A tight hour can return no clips even when the rest of that day has matches. Showing the stored caption, instead of asking another model to retell the clip, keeps the person looking at the actual footage.

title: The Street Talks Back
summary: We take street camera images of vehicles and see how compatible they are as a dating pair (tinder for vehicles)
description:
This is a dating app for vehicles. We take street camera footage, detct and track the vehicles in it and give each one profile built from it how it behaves. Compatibility is computed on the video not just narrated by a LLM. We score things on what the footage shows: speed and driving lanes, times of day etc. The LLM explains the score instead of inventing it so every claim traces back to a clip
**Ingest:** Street footage is loaded and indexed so it can be searched and streamed by timestamp
**Track:** YOLO detects and tracks vehicles frame to frame, producing a track history for each one (path, speed, dwell time, proximity to others).
**Understand:** Cosmos describes each vehicle’s behavior and its interactions with other vehicles (“yields to cyclists,” “idles at the curb”).
**Profile:** An LLM turns the track data and Cosmos descriptions into a bio, a nickname, and personality traits
**Match:** A scoring function compares track features for each pair of vehicles. Pairs that shared a clip or camera are candidates
**Explain and chat:** An LLM writes the compatibility breakdown and a “first date,” and vehicle personas chat with their matches and accept or reject based on their profiles
VAST  We read indexed data, stream the clips and persists complaints and tickets Nvidia - Cosmos reasons captions aree the evidence. YOLO waks the judge cosmos embed runs search and interview

title: UnfoldUnrest
summary: UnfoldUnrest turns everyday bike footage into a street safety audit: it finds crossings where hedges, planters or parked cars hide people about to cross from an approaching rider, says what to change, and backs every finding with the frames and a traced AI check.
description:
The problem
At a crossing, a person on a bike needs to see who is about to step out, early enough to stop. Hedges, planters, kiosks and parked cars set right up to the crossing take that view away. Cities fix this by daylighting, clearing the space before crossings, but finding the bad corners takes site visits and complaints, and those checks happen from a driver’s or walker’s eye, not the bike lane.

What it does
UnfoldUnrest turns ordinary first-person ride video into that audit. It rebuilds the street in 3D, finds the crossings and everything around them, and asks one question at each: could the rider see both sides in time? Where they couldn’t, it names what was in the way, suggests the fix, and shows the frames that prove it.
The value
Every ride becomes a survey. Planners get specific corners and objects to act on instead of a general call for safer streets. Advocates get evidence they can point to. Riders learn which crossings to slow down for. It needs only a camera, so it reaches any street people ride.
How the sponsor tools fitW&B Inference runs a vision model as an independent second opinion: the 3D check makes a claim, and the model looks at the real frames and confirms or rejects it, so whoever acts on a finding can trust it. Weave traces every stage, prompt, image and answer, so each finding can be followed back to its footage and reasoning. Clips arrive from the VAST environment carrying their source, so every result traces to the video it came from.

title: Warehouse best buddy
summary: A real-time video agent for warehouse safety and operations. It watches every camera through the VSS stack on VAST, catches near misses between workers and forklifts, finds idle labor and idle machines, prices the idle time per shift, and answers questions with cited clips.
description:
For warehouse safety managers and operations leads: the cameras already record every shift, but nobody has time to watch them.

Real time: every 30 s the agent checks what VSS has indexed, analyzes new footage once it is fully indexed, and the app updates within seconds.

Safety you can trust: motion tracks from the YOLO detections propose candidate near misses, NVIDIA Cosmos Reason checks that exact time window and image region, and the camera views vote. Asked directly, Cosmos called 168 of 180 clips a near miss, so the agent never relies on that question. With verification, 0 of 12 random control moments were flagged and all 3 drill near misses were caught.

Operations: idle labor, idle machines, congestion and underused zones, with recommendations tied to the evidence and an idle-cost estimate with editable assumptions (about $859 recoverable per shift, about $215k a year at the defaults).

Ask and report: plain-English questions answered by NVIDIA Nemotron-3-Ultra on W&B Inference, grounded in the analyzer's facts and VSS search, citing alerts and clips. Every number in the shift report is checked against the data.

Results go back to VastDB (alerts, flags, per-segment metrics), keyed by each segment's S3 URI, so they join with the VSS captions and embeddings.

Built with NVIDIA Cosmos Reason and Nemotron, VAST S3, DataEngine and VastDB, CoreWeave GPUs, W&B Inference and Cursor, on 60 videos from 33 camera views.

title: Spore
summary: Spore helps video model operators find gaps in their evaluation data, grow synthetic data to cover those conditions, and build new evals and benchmarks for training improved models.
description: Video AI fails quietly on conditions your cameras don’t see often. Spore finds those gaps, grows synthetic data to cover them, and turns that data into evals for training better models. Spore searched VAST’s video index for missing conditions: the highway cameras have 30 clips, mostly clear daylight, and none at night, in rain, in heavy fog or in snow. An LLM on W&B Inference, traced in Weave, ranks which gaps matter. Spore grows the missing weather onto real clips with a physics weather layer and NVIDIA Cosmos Transfer. The cars stay in place, so the labels carry over and testing runs automatically. On CoreWeave GPUs, it tests the models in the VSS pipeline: in light fog, YOLO finds only four in ten visible cars, while Cosmos Reason keeps counting them. The result is a new benchmark and training set for better models.

summary: AURAAFIT turns street-camera video into outfit analytics a merchandiser can act on: what people wear and carry, with a VAST clip and a W&B Weave trace behind every label, and without guessing who anyone is.
description:
Stores count foot traffic, but they can't see what the street is wearing. AURAAFIT reads outfits from video.

It starts from event footage indexed in VAST VSS (612 clips, 13 cameras). NVIDIA YOLO11 finds and tracks each person, and W&B Inference vision (Gemma 4) labels what they wear and carry: top, bottom, outer layer, bags. Every labelling call is traced in W&B Weave. Requiring a real garment type in our prompt took typed labels from 49 to 213 out of 214. NVIDIA Cosmos3-Reason adds a scene caption for each 5-second piece.

The app at auraafit.tech replays recorded street cameras from San Francisco and New York with the labels on the boxes. Buyers can search the labels ("backpack"), and each match links to its clip and timestamp in VAST. A dashboard rolls up 214 person-sightings into colour mix, style mix and carried items, with CSV export. A merchandising agent reads only the totals and drafts store actions, such as putting carry accessories near the entrance because 32% of sightings carry a backpack.

Privacy by design: a guard filter keeps clothing and carried items only. Age, gender, race and faces are never inferred, and nothing is tracked across cameras. Counts are sightings, not unique people.

Built for retailers, landlords and business districts deciding what to stock or lease on a block. Next step: a consenting storefront camera, over repeated days.

title: Nostradamus
summary: Prediction markets on the next five seconds of video
description: Nostradamus turns an indexed archive of video footage into a live prediction market. Each round plays one 5-second video segment and asks a single question about the next five seconds, rotating between pedestrians, vehicles, and intersections. A Weights & Biases model reads only the current clip's caption and quotes an opening price in cents, with its reasoning shown. You buy Yes or No at that price, choosing how many contracts, then settle: the following indexed segment plays, W&B judges it from that caption alone, and your buying power moves by M$1 per contract. The same question is listed as a real play-money binary on Manifold, opened at the model's price, bet on your behalf, and resolved from the clip.

title: BLACKBOX
summary: A robot-fleet black box that replays a drive in Rerun with tracks, closeness, time to contact, and Cosmos event times.
description:
BLACKBOX is a fleet black box on the VAST video stack. After a close call, the camera, the objects, the distance, and the model's read are on one clock.

The App button opens this page. The Rerun viewer plays Toronto AV drive 01, 13:25–14:00. That recording holds each clip as video, YOLO tracks and one-second trails, in-path proximity for people, bicycles, and vehicles, a time-to-contact lane, and Cosmos3-Reason event lines on the risk-2 clips.

On the 13:55 clip the ego car is slowing on a narrow street. The recording has 65 tracks. A bicycle in the centre path reaches proximity 0.84. The shortest time to contact is 1.8 seconds, on a car. Cosmos times a pedestrian in the path at 13:55, 13:56, 13:58, and 13:59. The stored caption says cyclist.

We did not build the video stack. VAST stores the clips and the index. Cosmos captions each five-second segment. YOLO writes the boxes. Rerun supplies the viewer. We added the episode view, the exporter, the tracks, proximity, time to contact, and the Cosmos timing pass.

Risk and event names on 13:55 are still inferred. Re-ingest has replaced 2 of 6 clips on each of the two parent chunks, and 13:55 still has the old caption.

title: CrossWise
summary: CrossWise is a crossing copilot for sidewalk delivery robots that watches street video and decides GO, WAIT or NO-GO every 0.2 seconds, so robots stop getting stuck at crosswalks.
description:
**Problem**. Delivery robots get stuck at crosswalks: they spin in place, miss the walk phase, or start into traffic.

**What it does**. CrossWise watches street video and decides GO, WAIT or NO-GO every 0.2 seconds, with the evidence drawn on the video. When a robot would wait too long, it escalates to a reroute or a remote operator. A scorecard ranks 7 crossings by difficulty for route planning.

**How it works**. Vehicles are tracked from the YOLO11 boxes VAST stores for every frame, with camera-shake removal and 1.5-second path prediction. The pedestrian signal is read from pixels. A vision model on W&B Inference finds cones, barriers and the free path. Unclear evidence forces WAIT. NVIDIA Cosmos Reason captions and Cosmos Embed search, on CoreWeave GPUs, found the crossing footage in the VAST archive. Decisions are stored in VastDB and model calls are traced in W&B Weave.

**What we learned**. Our first version had an LLM judge 5-second captions. It confused the car light with the pedestrian signal and parked cars with traffic. We rebuilt the core as frame-level perception and measured both on 5 clips: starts against DON'T WALK fell from 3 to 0, crossings rose from 6 to 8, and time from WALK to rolling dropped from 3.4 s to 1.0 s.

Limits. Decision support on recorded footage; it does not control a robot. Built end to end with Cursor.
